results.summary_before: This project combines four sub-designs—a shift register, a hexadecimal seven-segment encoder, a 1-bit ALU, and a 3-bit adder—selectable via two project-select pins. The remaining six inputs are used for data and control depending on the selected mode, and outputs drive a 7-segment display or provide results. It is built for the Wokwi simulator and is intended as a multi-purpose educational tool. No silicon test results are reported.

results.summary_before: This is a Simon Says memory game where the user must repeat an ever-growing sequence of colors, each associated with a tone. The sequence is shown on four LEDs and played through a speaker, and the user responds using four buttons. The game supports four clock speeds selected by two inputs, and it plays level-up and game-over sounds. It requires external hardware including four push buttons with pull-down resistors, four LEDs, and optionally a speaker or buzzer.

It requires external VGA connections with resistors, buttons, and an optional speaker.

results.summary_before: This project implements a two-player Pong game in Verilog, outputting a 2-bit-per-channel VGA video signal and a sound output. Each player controls a paddle with three buttons (left, right, action), and the game ends when one player runs out of lives. The design uses a VGA timing module and painter modules to generate graphics and detect collisions, with the ball bouncing at different angles depending on where it hits the paddle. It requires a VGA monitor, a VGA DAC built from 2-bit R2R resistor networks, and external buttons; the author reports that the silicon works.

results.summary_before: This is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, featuring three square wave tone generators and one noise generator with white and periodic noise. It is programmed via an 8-bit data bus and provides both digital 8-bit audio output and PWM output for analog audio. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are needed to produce sound. The design is well-documented, includes a test suite, and aims for hardware preservation and education.

results.summary_before: This design is a monophonic synth voice with two oscillators, a second-order low-pass filter, and programmable sweep rates that act as simple envelopes. It is controlled through a register interface written over eight data pins, four address pins and a write strobe, and it outputs audio both as a PWM signal and as an 8-bit sample for reconstruction with a resistor ladder. The oscillators use a floating-point-style period format to emulate the exponential volt-per-octave response of analog synths, and the filter uses a shared barrel shifter instead of multipliers. Silicon tests report that the registers can be written and that a demo tune plays back correctly, and it needs an external audio connection with a voltage divider to protect the audio device.
